claims.assertion: The driver drove 24.7 km against a 21.6 km optimal route, an excess of 3.2 km (+15%), which the rider was billed for on a metered RydeTAXI trip.
The excess is not noise from map-matching: a single off-route segment 09:32–09:38 put the car 2.96 km of driving on roads the optimal route does not use, reaching up to 974 m away from it.

That segment is not exempt; the driver's own statement that 'my GPS rerouted me' offers no traffic cause, and the only recorded conditions on the optimal route are moderate speed bands 4 (30–39 km/h) with no incident anywhere near the route.
The reroute was not agreed in advance: there is no in-app chat at all between rider and driver, so there is no rider consent timestamp preceding the 09:32 segment start.
Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted detour kilometres entered the fare; at the billed $1.41/km the 2.96 km detour segment corresponds to $4.17 in extra distance charges.
The fare already itemises $4.45 of excess-distance billing for the full 3.2 km gap, confirming the meter charged for the detour rather than absorbing it in a fixed quote.

The driver has 1 upheld dispute in 90 days and 2 disputes total; if the tribunal accepts a fresh upheld route finding here, RD-6's repeated-violation flag is engaged on his account, not on the rider's (rider: 1 dispute, 0 upheld).

weaknesses: The gps record shows 3.2 km of excess overall (F1) but only 2.96 km is attributable to the single off-route segment (F3); the driver will argue the ~0.25 km residual is map-matching error and outside RD-2, and RD-2 expressly does not refund that residual — so the recoverable base is 2.96 km, not the full 3.2 km.

The driver's case will rely on his statement (F8) that GPS rerouting was legitimate, plus the trip's real delays: 21.4 minutes over estimate (F2) and speed band 4 on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (F9, F10, F11) — he will say he was choosing the faster route as Ryde permits, and our answer is that RD-4 requires an incident on the replaced optimal segment, which F11 says does not exist.
The rider's own 90-day record shows 1 dispute with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver can use to paint this as a second unfounded complaint.

The metered-fare breakdown (F6) shows time charges of $12.96 for 49.8 minutes, so the driver may claim the trip was slow rather than long; we do not contest the waiting/time units, only the detour distance.

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered trip (F6 shows a metered breakdown of base + distance + time) billed 24.7 km against a 21.6 km optimal route; the meter is driven by distance units, so any excess distance is the only refundable element.
Only one off-route segment exists: 09:32–09:38, 2.96 km added (F3). The remaining 0.2 km of the 3.2 km total excess (F1) is map-matching residual and must not be refunded under RD-2.

My client's reroute is justified by congestion on the optimal route: the optimal corridor EAST COAST PARKWAY was recording speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) throughout 08:58–10:01, covering the 09:32–09:38 segment window (F9).

AIRPORT BOULEVARD, the category-2 approach to the destination, was likewise at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) over the same window (F10), corroborating that the diversion was driven by real congestion rather than by my client's preference.

No traffic incidents were recorded near the route and weather was Fair with 0.0 mm rain (F11, F12), which means the tie-break must rest on the speed-band evidence in F9 and F10 rather than on any incident record.

There is no chat agreement to point to because no in-app messages were exchanged (F7); the rider was therefore never charged for any agreed stop or destination change, and no $3.00 or extra stop charge appears in the bill (F6).

The waiting line on the bill is $0.00 and there is no undeclared surcharge in the total of $53.17 (F6), so the only contested money is the distance element, which on the driver's side should be limited to the map-matching residual rather than the full 3.2 km.

My client's record shows 968 trips in 90 days with only 2 disputes and 0 route disputes upheld (F14), which is inconsistent with a pattern of deliberate detouring and is a reason not to attach any repeated-breach account flag.

weaknesses: The GPS record in F3 shows an off-route segment of 2.96 km that no contractual or passenger-requested stop explains (F7 has no chat), so RD-1 is breached on that segment and at least part of the refund is unavoidable.

My RD-4 congestion argument is built only on speed-band evidence (F9, F10); RD-4(a) requires an incident record and F11 states no incidents were recorded, so the rider will argue R-4(b) band evidence cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The rider will rely on F1 (+3.2 km, +15%) and F2 (+21.4 min over estimate) to argue the whole detour was avoidable, and on F4 ($4.45 of billed excess) to claim the full amount back rather than only the 2.96 km.
The driver statement in F8 asserts 'nothing wrong with the fare' with no supporting record, and under the record-first rule it cannot outweigh the GPS off-route segment in F3.

events.body:
→ D1 (concedes): Accepted as far as it goes: the meter is distance-driven on RydeTAXI, which is exactly why the detour kilometres are recoverable, and RD-2's metered branch refunds the unexempted segment km. The billed excess of $4.45 over 3.2 km (F4, F6) confirms distance entered the fare rather than being absorbed. [F1 F4 F6] [RD-2 RD-1]
→ D2 (concedes): Conceded: RD-2 expressly does not refund the residual between the excess-distance billing and the sum of segments, so we rest on the 2.96 km in F3 and claim 2.96 × $1.41 = $4.17, not the full $4.45. That is the figure in our requested outcome. [F1 F3 F4] [RD-2]
→ D3: Band 4 is 30–39 km/h, defined by LTA as moderate flow and nowhere near the band 1–2 (0–9 / 10–19 km/h) congestion bands; RD-4(b) only lets band evidence corroborate an incident, and RD-4(b) states band evidence standing alone does not exempt a segment in this system. [F9] [RD-4]
→ D4: Airport Boulevard is category-2 traffic already inside the destination approach, not evidence about the replaced portion of the optimal route, and under RD-4 the corroboration must target the substituted segment; F10 therefore corroborates nothing about the 09:32–09:38 diversion. [F3 F10] [RD-4]
→ D5: F11 (no incidents recorded) is fatal to the driver's exemption rather than neutral: RD-4(a) requires an incident within 300 m of the optimal route, reported before the segment and still listed during the trip, and RD-4(c) sends an unmatched segment straight back to RD-2. Fair weather in F12 removes weather as an alternative reasonable cause. [F11 F12 F3] [RD-4]
→ D6: We agree there was no agreement — and that is the rider's point, not the driver's: with no chat at all (F7), nothing satisfies RD-5's requirement that consent precede the 09:32 segment start in F3, so the segment stands unexempted. RD-3 is irrelevant here because no stop or destination change was ever requested or charged (F6). [F3 F6 F7] [RD-5 RD-3]
→ D7: The rider does not contest the $5.00 waiting fee or any surcharge — F6 shows $0.00 waiting and a 1.0× surge in F5 — so the driver's point concedes the whole field in dispute: distance. On distance the meter charged $34.84 for 24.7 km, of which 2.96 km was unexempted detour (F3, F6), giving $4.17. [F3 F5 F6] [RD-2 FARE-1]
→ D8: We do not seek an account flag on volume alone; but F14 shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld in 90 days, and RD-6 triggers on an upheld route finding plus a prior upheld dispute, so the flag question turns on whether the tribunal upholds this segment, not on the driver's trip count. [F14 F13] [RD-6]
→ C1: No change: we maintain the route-deviation finding, narrowed to the single unexempted segment in F3, refund 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17, which is computable from F3 (extra_km) and F6 (distance fare ÷ distance km). [F1 F3 F6] [RD-1 RD-2]
Revised ask: refund_partial $4.17

points.response: Accepted as far as it goes: the meter is distance-driven on RydeTAXI, which is exactly why the detour kilometres are recoverable, and RD-2's metered branch refunds the unexempted segment km. The billed excess of $4.45 over 3.2 km (F4, F6) confirms distance entered the fare rather than being absorbed.

Conceded: RD-2 expressly does not refund the residual between the excess-distance billing and the sum of segments, so we rest on the 2.96 km in F3 and claim 2.96 × $1.41 = $4.17, not the full $4.45. That is the figure in our requested outcome.

Band 4 is 30–39 km/h, defined by LTA as moderate flow and nowhere near the band 1–2 (0–9 / 10–19 km/h) congestion bands; RD-4(b) only lets band evidence corroborate an incident, and RD-4(b) states band evidence standing alone does not exempt a segment in this system.

Airport Boulevard is category-2 traffic already inside the destination approach, not evidence about the replaced portion of the optimal route, and under RD-4 the corroboration must target the substituted segment; F10 therefore corroborates nothing about the 09:32–09:38 diversion.

F11 (no incidents recorded) is fatal to the driver's exemption rather than neutral: RD-4(a) requires an incident within 300 m of the optimal route, reported before the segment and still listed during the trip, and RD-4(c) sends an unmatched segment straight back to RD-2. Fair weather in F12 removes weather as an alternative reasonable cause.

We agree there was no agreement — and that is the rider's point, not the driver's: with no chat at all (F7), nothing satisfies RD-5's requirement that consent precede the 09:32 segment start in F3, so the segment stands unexempted. RD-3 is irrelevant here because no stop or destination change was ever requested or charged (F6).

The rider does not contest the $5.00 waiting fee or any surcharge — F6 shows $0.00 waiting and a 1.0× surge in F5 — so the driver's point concedes the whole field in dispute: distance. On distance the meter charged $34.84 for 24.7 km, of which 2.96 km was unexempted detour (F3, F6), giving $4.17.

We do not seek an account flag on volume alone; but F14 shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld in 90 days, and RD-6 triggers on an upheld route finding plus a prior upheld dispute, so the flag question turns on whether the tribunal upholds this segment, not on the driver's trip count.

No change: we maintain the route-deviation finding, narrowed to the single unexempted segment in F3, refund 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17, which is computable from F3 (extra_km) and F6 (distance fare ÷ distance km).

events.body:

what_would_change: Had an LTA incident been recorded on the stretch F3 replaced, before it started, RD-4 would exempt it (−$4.17).
Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The driver drove 24.7 km against a 21.6 km optimal route, an excess of 3.2 km (+15%), which the rider was billed for on a metered RydeTAXI trip.
The excess is not noise from map-matching: a single off-route segment 09:32–09:38 put the car 2.96 km of driving on roads the optimal route does not use, reaching up to 974 m away from it.

That segment is not exempt; the driver's own statement that 'my GPS rerouted me' offers no traffic cause, and the only recorded conditions on the optimal route are moderate speed bands 4 (30–39 km/h) with no incident anywhere near the route.
The reroute was not agreed in advance: there is no in-app chat at all between rider and driver, so there is no rider consent timestamp preceding the 09:32 segment start.
Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted detour kilometres entered the fare; at the billed $1.41/km the 2.96 km detour segment corresponds to $4.17 in extra distance charges.
The fare already itemises $4.45 of excess-distance billing for the full 3.2 km gap, confirming the meter charged for the detour rather than absorbing it in a fixed quote.

The driver has 1 upheld dispute in 90 days and 2 disputes total; if the tribunal accepts a fresh upheld route finding here, RD-6's repeated-violation flag is engaged on his account, not on the rider's (rider: 1 dispute, 0 upheld).

weaknesses: The gps record shows 3.2 km of excess overall (F1) but only 2.96 km is attributable to the single off-route segment (F3); the driver will argue the ~0.25 km residual is map-matching error and outside RD-2, and RD-2 expressly does not refund that residual — so the recoverable base is 2.96 km, not the full 3.2 km.

The driver's case will rely on his statement (F8) that GPS rerouting was legitimate, plus the trip's real delays: 21.4 minutes over estimate (F2) and speed band 4 on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (F9, F10, F11) — he will say he was choosing the faster route as Ryde permits, and our answer is that RD-4 requires an incident on the replaced optimal segment, which F11 says does not exist.
The rider's own 90-day record shows 1 dispute with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver can use to paint this as a second unfounded complaint.

The metered-fare breakdown (F6) shows time charges of $12.96 for 49.8 minutes, so the driver may claim the trip was slow rather than long; we do not contest the waiting/time units, only the detour distance.

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered trip (F6 shows a metered breakdown of base + distance + time) billed 24.7 km against a 21.6 km optimal route; the meter is driven by distance units, so any excess distance is the only refundable element.
Only one off-route segment exists: 09:32–09:38, 2.96 km added (F3). The remaining 0.2 km of the 3.2 km total excess (F1) is map-matching residual and must not be refunded under RD-2.

My client's reroute is justified by congestion on the optimal route: the optimal corridor EAST COAST PARKWAY was recording speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) throughout 08:58–10:01, covering the 09:32–09:38 segment window (F9).

AIRPORT BOULEVARD, the category-2 approach to the destination, was likewise at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) over the same window (F10), corroborating that the diversion was driven by real congestion rather than by my client's preference.

No traffic incidents were recorded near the route and weather was Fair with 0.0 mm rain (F11, F12), which means the tie-break must rest on the speed-band evidence in F9 and F10 rather than on any incident record.

There is no chat agreement to point to because no in-app messages were exchanged (F7); the rider was therefore never charged for any agreed stop or destination change, and no $3.00 or extra stop charge appears in the bill (F6).

The waiting line on the bill is $0.00 and there is no undeclared surcharge in the total of $53.17 (F6), so the only contested money is the distance element, which on the driver's side should be limited to the map-matching residual rather than the full 3.2 km.

My client's record shows 968 trips in 90 days with only 2 disputes and 0 route disputes upheld (F14), which is inconsistent with a pattern of deliberate detouring and is a reason not to attach any repeated-breach account flag.

weaknesses: The GPS record in F3 shows an off-route segment of 2.96 km that no contractual or passenger-requested stop explains (F7 has no chat), so RD-1 is breached on that segment and at least part of the refund is unavoidable.

My RD-4 congestion argument is built only on speed-band evidence (F9, F10); RD-4(a) requires an incident record and F11 states no incidents were recorded, so the rider will argue R-4(b) band evidence cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The rider will rely on F1 (+3.2 km, +15%) and F2 (+21.4 min over estimate) to argue the whole detour was avoidable, and on F4 ($4.45 of billed excess) to claim the full amount back rather than only the 2.96 km.
The driver statement in F8 asserts 'nothing wrong with the fare' with no supporting record, and under the record-first rule it cannot outweigh the GPS off-route segment in F3.

points.response: Accepted as far as it goes: the meter is distance-driven on RydeTAXI, which is exactly why the detour kilometres are recoverable, and RD-2's metered branch refunds the unexempted segment km. The billed excess of $4.45 over 3.2 km (F4, F6) confirms distance entered the fare rather than being absorbed.

Conceded: RD-2 expressly does not refund the residual between the excess-distance billing and the sum of segments, so we rest on the 2.96 km in F3 and claim 2.96 × $1.41 = $4.17, not the full $4.45. That is the figure in our requested outcome.

Band 4 is 30–39 km/h, defined by LTA as moderate flow and nowhere near the band 1–2 (0–9 / 10–19 km/h) congestion bands; RD-4(b) only lets band evidence corroborate an incident, and RD-4(b) states band evidence standing alone does not exempt a segment in this system.

Airport Boulevard is category-2 traffic already inside the destination approach, not evidence about the replaced portion of the optimal route, and under RD-4 the corroboration must target the substituted segment; F10 therefore corroborates nothing about the 09:32–09:38 diversion.

F11 (no incidents recorded) is fatal to the driver's exemption rather than neutral: RD-4(a) requires an incident within 300 m of the optimal route, reported before the segment and still listed during the trip, and RD-4(c) sends an unmatched segment straight back to RD-2. Fair weather in F12 removes weather as an alternative reasonable cause.

We agree there was no agreement — and that is the rider's point, not the driver's: with no chat at all (F7), nothing satisfies RD-5's requirement that consent precede the 09:32 segment start in F3, so the segment stands unexempted. RD-3 is irrelevant here because no stop or destination change was ever requested or charged (F6).

The rider does not contest the $5.00 waiting fee or any surcharge — F6 shows $0.00 waiting and a 1.0× surge in F5 — so the driver's point concedes the whole field in dispute: distance. On distance the meter charged $34.84 for 24.7 km, of which 2.96 km was unexempted detour (F3, F6), giving $4.17.

We do not seek an account flag on volume alone; but F14 shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld in 90 days, and RD-6 triggers on an upheld route finding plus a prior upheld dispute, so the flag question turns on whether the tribunal upholds this segment, not on the driver's trip count.

No change: we maintain the route-deviation finding, narrowed to the single unexempted segment in F3, refund 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17, which is computable from F3 (extra_km) and F6 (distance fare ÷ distance km).

Conceded as to the arithmetic: F1 shows +3.2 km against the 21.6 km optimal route on a metered RydeTAXI trip billed by distance units, so some distance excess is refundable — but only the exempted/unexempted segment split under RD-2 governs the amount, not the headline 3.2 km.
Accepted that the 2.96 km off-route segment in F3 is a real detour and not map-matching noise; RD-1 places the shortest-direct-route duty on the driver, so this segment is the correct unit of review.

I do not rely on the statement in F8 — the system record shows the optimal corridor EAST COAST PARKWAY at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) for 08:58–10:01 and AIRPORT BOULEVARD likewise (F9, F10), the bands do not cover a justified reroute on their own, so see my concession below.

Neither side has chat evidence: F7 records no in-app messages at all, so RD-5 cannot be satisfied by either party, but the absence of rider consent also means the $3.00 change-of-destination fee and any stop charge were correctly never levied (F6).

The $4.17 figure itself is the one point of the rider's brief I can live with: F3's 2.96 km at the billed $1.41/km rate used in F4 is the only computation consistent with RD-2's rule of refunding distance units of the unexempted segment.

F6 shows the $4.45 excess-distance line covers the full 3.2 km gap while only 2.96 km is attributable to a segment (F3), and RD-2 expressly does not refund the residual difference, so the refundable base is $4.17, not $4.45.

F14 shows my client's own 90-day record contains 0 upheld route disputes despite 968 trips, so a single fresh route finding does not make this 'repeated' conduct; the 1 upheld entry is not a route matter and RD-6 flags only where the count is met, while any flag would attach to the account under review, not to the rider.
